newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Sao Paulo streets fill to welcome Japan's emperor.
newsitem.headline: Sao Paulo streets fill to welcome Japan's emperor.

text.p: Thousands of Brazilians of Japanese descent stood in the rain to catch a glimpse of Emperor Akihito and Empress Michiko as their motorcade passed through the streets of Sao Paulo, home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan.
The imperial couple, midway through a 10-day day visit to Brazil, were greeted by about 5,000 people who crammed onto the narrow streets of Libderdade, the city's Japanese neighbourhood.
The crowd cheered and waved Brazilian and Japanese flags to recognise the first Japanese imperial visit to Latin America.
Earlier in the day the imperial couple were greeted with shouts of "Banzai," Japan's national patriotic cry, from some 8,000 Japanese-Brazilians who packed into a gymnasium.
In a brief message, Akihito praised the courage and determination of Japanese immigrants who began arriving in Brazil 90 years ago to farm its vast interior.
"Thank you Brazil, for accepting our people so warmly," Akihito said.
As Akihito entered the gymnasium he was stopped by an elderly farmer who said it was the first Thursday he had taken off work in his life. "I did this to see you," the farmer said.

After the reception, a woman who appeared to be in her 60s slipped by a security line and tried to give Akihito a letter before being pulled away by guards. She was apparently trying to give the emperor a letter that she claimed proved her lineage to Japan's imperial family.
Sao Paulo, Brazil's sprawling metropolis and industrial capital, is home to most of the 1.3 million Brazilians of Japanese descent.

While most of the early Japanese immigrants cleared forests for coffee cultivation in the interior of Sao Paulo, many later migrated to the city where they opened small businesses and started professional practices.
Today, after decades of booming economic growth in Japan, thousands of Japanese-Brazilians have opted to return to their ancestral homeland in a reverse bid to improve their lives.

Some 170,000 'dekassegui,' or Japanese Brazilians working in Japan, sent home $4 billion in 1995. The flows are so steady that federal bank Banco do Brasil used the remittances to guarantee a bond issue last year.
The dekassegui, which number 200,000, have complained they are treated as second-class citizens in Japan. But Akihito said his nation valued their contributions.
Brazil and Japan are key trading partners, with some $6.5 billion in goods traded in 1995. Japan also provides Brazil with technical and financial aid.
The imperial couple placed flowers at a mausoleum of early Japanese immigrants and visited a museum of Japanese history in Brazil. They were to attend a soccer match later on Thursday.
Akihito and Michiko are in Brazil until Monday, when they will fly to Buenos Aires for a three-day visit to Argentina.
